compression.title: Schoenberg Database of Manuscripts
compression.lede: is the Schoenberg Institute for Manuscript Studies' crowd-sourced database of observations of pre-modern manuscripts in sales, auction and collection catalogues (its pages; MMM white paper), recording sale, location and ownership and testing none of it (provenance census record).

sentences.text: The Schoenberg Database of Manuscripts (SDBM, sdbm.library.upenn.edu) is "an online, user-maintained, open-access, collaborative rese[arch …]" in the words of its operator's page on the Penn Libraries site (Penn Libraries, Digital Projects, snippet only), and a database in the lineage of manuscripts and books that attaches provenance to "an observation of a pre-modern manuscript in a catalogue, inventory or other source" (provenance census record).

Its home page states what it does: it "continuously aggregates and updates historic observations of pre-modern manuscripts drawn from over 14,000 auction and sales catalogs, inventories, catalogs from institutional and private collections, and other sources that document the sales and locations of these books from around the world" (SDBM home page); the same sentence stands with "over 13,000" in Lisa Fagin Davis's entry of 26 August 2015 for the Medieval Academy's Medieval Digital Resources (MDR), and with 14,000 but without "historic" in the copy Chuck Jones reprinted on AWOL on 10 May 2020 (AWOL).

Medieval Digital Resources classes it as a catalogue, a crowd-sourced database, downloadable data, Linked Open Data, a relational database and a searchable database (MDR), and the Capture Registry records it as not the archive's, run by the Schoenberg Institute for Manuscript Studies, University of Pennsylvania (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The census record names the same operator (provenance census record); the Institute's pages on the Penn Libraries site list the SDBM among its digital projects (Penn Libraries, snippet only) and say that "At the core of SIMS is the Lawrence J. Schoenberg collection of manuscripts, which was donated to the Penn Libraries in 2011" (About SIMS, snippet only), and Penn Press announces that the current and back content of the journal Manuscript Studies is to become fully Open Access (Penn Press, title and snippet only).

The Lawrence J. Schoenberg Collection on the same rail is the collection and not the database: "Nearly 300 manuscripts and documents dating from ca. 1900 BC to the 20th century" (Penn Libraries, snippet only).

The unit is the observation: the Mapping Manuscript Migrations white paper, written by the project team with the Institute's staff among its authors, contrasts Bibale, which "takes a single manuscript as the basic unit", with the SDBM, which "focuses on an “observation” of a manuscript in a sales or auction catalogue or collection catalogue" and "consists of records which are observations of a manuscript at a point in time", two or more linked by a "manuscript record" (MMM white paper), and the census record gives the unit as "an observation (an entry in a source that documents a manuscript)" (provenance census record).

The Capture Registry finds the unit held in the composition at the address, entries as observations linked under manuscript records, "the record's unit" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and the home page's menus name an SDBM Name Authority, an SDBM Place Authority, an Entity Relationship Diagram and a SPARQL Data Model (SDBM home page).

In the census record's terms the SDBM records provenance: its capability is "records" among the schema's expresses, records and tests, the relations it carries are sale, location and ownership, its carrier is "observation records with a VIAF-based name authority", and under the schema's rule that "Untested capability reads 'not tested'" it carries no tested transformation and no retention result, the record asking of it what it asks of every resource: "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" (provenance census record).

Its own pages name those carriers, a "VIAF-based Name Authority", "Enhanced Provenance data" and a SPARQL endpoint (SDBM home page; AWOL's 2020 copy), and its provenance facet as read is headed by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (23,741), Sir Thomas Phillipps (21,582) and the British Library (7,822) (SDBM home page).

The white paper records what the name authority lacked and gained: the Institute "is ineligible to participate" in VIAF, "despite offering to contribute", and through MMM "hundreds of personal and institutional names have been corrected for authority control" in the Schoenberg Database and Bibale (MMM white paper).

Its relations of sale, location and ownership (provenance census record) are those of what the MMM data paper calls a specialist database focused on "the history and provenance of medieval and Renaissance manuscripts" (JOHD 2020), and the archive dates that provenance as centuries old: "Provenance" is "a centuries-old concept in archival science, art history, and legal evidence", and art-historical provenance, "Documented chain of ownership and attribution for art objects", is an "Adjacent tradition" to semantic provenance, "Same conceptual structure; different object" (#725).

#725 lists provenance's disciplinary homes, "art history (chain of ownership, attribution)" second among eight, and holds that "Each tradition answers a specific question about origin", the AI-era discourse sitting "at the intersection of the last four", which are data provenance, content authenticity, dataset documentation and digital preservation (#725).

Of archival provenance #725 says that "Archival theory has long insisted that provenance is contextual and meaning-bearing", that "An archival custody chain matters because it preserves the *meaning* of records", and that the value of preserved lineage "is realized only when the descendants of a work need to find their way back to its sources"; semantic provenance "extends archival concerns to circulating meaning under AI synthesis", and what AI synthesis introduces is "the first adversary capable of stripping that meaning dimension at machine scale" (#725).
#725 bounds its own frame: its three dimensions "reflect the current institutional landscape, not an ontological claim that provenance is exhausted by three categories" (#725).

#43 names the evidence provenance studies rests on and moves it: "Provenance studies stabilizes authorship and priority through archival evidence — manuscripts, signatures, watermarks, chain of custody", and retrocausal canon formation "extends provenance into the retrieval layer", where the DOI, the timestamp and the cross-linked citation network are "the digital equivalents of the watermark and the scribal hand" (#43); #610, by Rex Fraction, marks what a catalogue does not do: "A catalog records that a manuscript exists, where it is held, what it contains. It does not analyze the scribal tradition, the variant readings, or the politics of textual transmission" (#610).

The counts are of sources and of records, and each carries its date: over 13,000 sources in the 2015 entry (MDR), over 14,000 in AWOL's 2020 copy and on the home page as read (AWOL; SDBM home page), "more than 240,000 records for manuscript observations" in MMM's data paper of May 2020 (JOHD 2020) and "240,000 records" in the white paper (MMM white paper).

The home page's source-type facet has its own figures: 122,751 collection catalogues, 99,319 auction and dealer catalogues and 19,859 unpublished sources in AWOL's copy of 2020, and 129,525, 106,401 and 23,861 on the page as read in 2026 (AWOL; SDBM home page), 241,929 and then 259,787 entries for those three types alone.

The census record gives the count as "over 14,000 auction and sales catalogs, inventories and other sources; 240,000 records (MMM white paper)" and lists "the current record count on the database itself" as not yet checked (provenance census record), and the Capture Registry finds the composition's two counts to be the record's two, "joined in one sentence" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It is built by its users: members are invited to "help us to build and maintain this resource" and to contribute their "own personal observations of a manuscript or group of manuscripts" singly or by batch upload (SDBM home page; MDR), which the census record states as continuous intake by registered users (provenance census record).

It may be searched or browsed "by author, title, seller, provenance, date, and others" and downloaded "in .xlsx or .csv format" (MDR), and the white paper reports a public SPARQL endpoint over "the pre-transformation RDF version of the data" (MMM white paper; the census record: search, download, SPARQL endpoint); MDR dates its content "500 - 1600" across Europe, the Middle East and East and South Asia (MDR), the period the Capture Registry records as unchecked against the census record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The condition of reuse is stated three ways: "Must provide credit" beside "No Fee" (MDR, 2015); "Download Search Results for your own use under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 Unported License" on the home page, reprinted by AWOL in 2020 (SDBM home page; AWOL); and "CC BY-SA 4.0 for downloaded search results" (provenance census record); MMM, which aggregates the SDBM, releases its own data "under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license" (JOHD 2020).
The Capture Registry finds the licence unsaid in the composition at the address: export given, the CC BY-SA 4.0 quote absent (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

MDR gives the project's status as ongoing (MDR); the home page dates the New SDBM's changes "As of April 1, 2017", made "thanks to input from the user community", and its recent-activity column as read shows its latest post, in the thread 'Ketterer Auctions - 30 November 2020', aged "over 2 years" (SDBM home page); the census record has it "active" (provenance census record).

The white paper states the database's limits: it "tracks generic titles rather than works in the specific sense employed by FRBR"; a manuscript's current location "is not specifically present in the Schoenberg Database, although it can often be inferred from the most recent observation"; its entries for sales and gifts "did not have place information associated with them"; and 6 of the 25 research questions could not be answered from it alone (MMM white paper).

The SDBM is one of the three source datasets of Mapping Manuscript Migrations, the 2017–2020 Digging into Data project that "took the data from three existing databases and turned them into Linked Open Data" (MMM white paper), in whose data paper of May 2020, the Institute's staff among its authors, an SDBM manuscript has a URI such as http://ldf.fi/mmm/manifestation_singleton/sdbm_784 and "The original data have not been corrected or amended in any way by the MMM project" (JOHD 2020); the census record carries the relation as part of mapping-manuscript-migrations (provenance census record).

The encyclopedia has no article on the database or its institute: the titles Schoenberg_Database_of_Manuscripts and Schoenberg_Institute_for_Manuscript_Studies answer HTTP 404, and the quoted name occurs in article space only as a cited source, in Black Hours, Morgan MS 493 and Sister Carrie (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29); the Bibliographical Society of America's channel carries an "Introduction to the Schoenberg Database of Manuscripts (SDBM)" (video card, title only).

At its address on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry reads the composition innocently first, the database and its host identified, what it traces and from how many sources and its structure laid out, and judges it "The best-composed of the census rows", host, unit, scale and structure "at the database's own grain", with "Only the licence, the condition of reuse," left out (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The Registry finds the Institute and Penn Libraries named in the composition and no person or identifier, a provenance erasure rate of 0.5, keeps the stray full stop of 'from more. than 14,000' as received, and notes that the census record landed the same day and that no card cites it, its findings checked against the census record and the pages it saved (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

O725-05.quote: All provenance has always had a semantic dimension *in principle*. An archival custody chain matters because it preserves the *meaning* of records.
